newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: POSTAL VOTES AN OPTION TO ELECT PEOPLE'S CONVENTION
Postal votes may be used to fulfil a federal Government promise, confirmed today, to allow the public to elect half the members of a people's convention to discuss proposals for a republic.
Prime Minister, John Howard, outlined the plan to Coalition MPs today.
They endorsed the Cabinet plan, which still has some detail to be worked through.
Under the plan, the people's constitutional convention would be held in November or December this year.
Mr Howard told Coalition M-Ps the Government would publish a discussion paper setting out a range of arguments, before the convention.
Sources say no Coalition M-Ps opposed the Cabinet plan, although some told the meeting there are more pressing priorities for Australia than the question of a republic.
QLD PREMIER EN ROUTE TO FLOODED SOUTH-WEST
The Queensland Premier, Rob Borbidge, says no limit will be placed on assistance for the flooded town of Charleville in the state's south-west.
Mr Borbidge has cut short a Cabinet meeting to fly to Charleville, and is due to arrive in the town shortly.
He's expected to announce an assistance package after an inspection of the town.
Water from the Warrego River is flowing through the town, and a gully which runs through the town centre has also burst its banks.
Emergency services personnel are sandbagging the town centre, and police have restricted access to the area.
It's expected that more than a thousand people will have been moved from their waterlogged homes by tonight.
WOODS' DEPARTURE MAY LEAVE COALITION IN A HOLE
New South Wales Liberal Senator, Bob Woods, may be encouraged to defer his planned resignation so the Coalition is not left a vote short in the Senate.
Senator Woods has announced he'll be quitting politics on March the first, citing family reasons.
He's also facing allegations concerning the misuse of Parliamentary expenses, with the Federal Police conducting an extensive investigation.

Although Senator Woods will be replaced by another Liberal member, the appointment needs to be ratified by a joint sitting of both houses of the New South Wales Parliament, which doesn't sit again until April.
That would leave the Coalition one Senator down for three sitting weeks, during which important legislation will be voted on.
The Government holds only 37 of the 76 Senate seats, having to rely on the cross-benches to achieve a majority.
A number of options are being considered, including persuading Senator Woods to delay his departure, or trying to strike a voting deal with the ALP that would maintain the status quo.
PROSECUTION PRESSES FOR HEAVY BOND SENTENCE
The Prosecution in the Alan Bond corporate fraud case has called for a substantial jail term to be imposed on the former tycoon.
Brian Martin QC, told the Supreme Court in Perth the offences were the largest fraud in Australia's corporate history and were deliberate, resulting in personal benefits to Bond.
Bond is facing a maximum five years jail on each of the charges to which he has pleaded guilty.
They relate to the transfer of hundreds of millions of dollars from Bell Resources to Bond Corporation in the late 1980s.
Earlier today, Bond's lawyer, Ian Callinan, concluded his submissions by saying his client was at risk physically and mentally.
Mr Callinan said that while the case was complex and difficult, Bond was remorseful and had made genuine attempts at rehabilitating himself.
The hearing is continuing.
POLITICIANS FORGET DIFFERENCE TO REMEMBER "GOOD BLOKE"
Senator John Panizza, who died last week, has been described as "a cheerful, lovable bloke", in tributes in federal parliament.
This assessment, by Prime Minister John Howard, was echoed by Opposition Leader, Kim Beazley.
Mr Beazley said Senator Panizza, a West Australian Liberal, was an authentic Australian success story.
Federal parliament's sitting for the first time this year, but the Senate will adjourn, after condolence motions, as a mark of respect.
Mr Howard told parliament Senator Panizza, who was a wheatgrower, was proud of his Italian heritage, but was "a 100 per cent lover of the Australian nation".
A memorial service for Senator Panizza will be held in Canberra next Tuesday.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
